d: The entity that controls the limited partnership and carries unlimited liability for its debts. Usually a special-purpose company owned by the fund's principals, it signs on behalf of the fund, makes investment decisions (often delegated to the manager) and receives carried interest.
x: A Delaware LLC acting as GP of a Delaware fund, owned by the four partners.
A Luxembourg Sàrl acting as general partner of an SCSp.
s: The fund is sued by a portfolio company's creditors.
The GP is the party with unlimited liability, which is why it is a limited company with few assets rather than the partners personally.
LPs vote to remove the GP under a no-fault clause.
A replacement GP is admitted and the outgoing GP's carry is usually cut or frozen as the LPA sets out.

d: An investor in the fund. LPs commit capital, receive reports and distributions, and vote on a limited list of matters such as LPA amendments, extensions and GP removal. Liability is capped at the commitment.
x: Pension funds, insurers, endowments, family offices, funds of funds, wealthy individuals.
A family office committing €10m across two VC funds and one buyout fund.
s: An LP wants to influence which deals the fund does.
It has no say in individual deals; influence comes through LPAC membership, co-investment rights and the re-up decision.
An LP is asked to return a distribution to cover an indemnity claim.
The LPA's giveback clause, usually capped and time-limited, decides whether it must pay.

d: The firm that runs the investment programme, employs the team and earns the management fee. It is often a separate entity from the GP for regulatory and tax reasons, appointed under an investment management agreement.
x: A London LLP advising a Luxembourg fund under an advisory agreement with the AIFM.
A Mumbai private limited company acting as investment manager of a SEBI AIF.
s: The GP and manager are separate entities.
Fees go to the manager; carry goes to the GP or carry vehicle. Regulators supervise the manager.
The manager's key partner leaves.
Key person provisions in the LPA may suspend investing until LPs approve a replacement.

d: The business that receives fees and pays salaries, office, travel, compliance and fundraising costs. A sustainable ManCo needs fee income that covers costs without depending on carry, and LPs check that fees are not a profit centre for large funds.
x: A €150m VC fund at 2% generates €3m a year to fund five partners and support staff.
A $3bn buyout fund where fee income far exceeds costs, prompting LP pushback on the fee rate.
s: Fund I at €50m cannot cover the team's costs at 2%.
Partners take lower salaries or the GP negotiates a budget-based fee in early years.
Fees rise faster than costs across Funds I–IV.
LPs negotiate lower rates or step-downs because fee profits weaken alignment with carry.

d: A manager authorised under AIFMD, legally responsible for portfolio and risk management of the AIF. It may delegate portfolio management (for example to an adviser outside the EU) under conditions that AIFMD II tightens.
x: A Luxembourg AIFM managing several RAIFs and delegating portfolio advice to managers in London and Mumbai.
A French portfolio management company authorised as AIFM by the AMF.
s: A Mumbai team runs a Luxembourg fund.
A Luxembourg AIFM holds the licence and delegates investment advice to the Mumbai team, keeping risk management in Luxembourg.
Regulator questions whether the AIFM is a letterbox.
It must show real oversight of delegates, with staff and resources to supervise them.

d: An authorised AIFM that provides its licence, risk management and compliance to managers who lack their own. Popular with first-time and non-EU managers launching EU funds.
x: A Luxembourg host AIFM onboarding a first-time venture manager's RAIF.
An Irish platform AIFM hosting a US manager's EU feeder.
s: A first-time team needs an EU fund in four months.
Using a host AIFM avoids a 6–12 month licence application.
The host AIFM vetoes a deal for risk reasons.
The AIFM has legal responsibility, so it can block transactions outside the risk framework.

d: The person or entity that sets up an Indian AIF. The sponsor or manager must hold the continuing interest, and both must meet SEBI's fit and proper criteria on an ongoing basis. The manager can also be the sponsor.
x: A private equity firm's Indian holding company acting as sponsor and manager.
A bank's subsidiary sponsoring an AIF managed by a separate asset manager.
s: A sponsor's net worth falls below what the continuing interest needs.
It must inform SEBI and put a remediation plan in place.
A sponsor tries to meet its continuing interest by waiving fees.
Not permitted; it must invest actual capital in the fund.

d: For AIFs set up as trusts, the trustee holds the assets for the beneficiaries and appoints the investment manager. Professional trustee companies usually fill this role and oversee compliance with the trust deed.
x: A trustee company holding the assets of a Cat II AIF.
A trustee signing the IMA appointing the manager.
s: Investors want to replace the manager.
They direct the trustee under the trust deed to terminate the IMA.
A conflict arises between manager and investors.
The trustee owes duties to beneficiaries and can intervene.

d: A SEBI-registered merchant banker files the AIF scheme's PPM with SEBI and carries out due diligence on it. SEBI comments are routed through the merchant banker.
x: An investment bank filing a Cat I VC scheme's PPM.
A merchant banker certifying PPM disclosures before launch.
s: SEBI raises comments on the PPM.
The merchant banker coordinates responses and refiles.
The manager changes key terms after filing.
Material changes go back through the merchant banker to SEBI.

d: The body, usually senior partners, that approves each new investment, follow-on and exit. The PPM describes who sits on it, how it votes and whether any member can veto.
x: A three-partner IC requiring unanimous approval.
An IC with an external adviser who has a vote on deals above €10m.
s: One partner is conflicted on a deal.
That partner recuses; the IC record shows the conflict and the vote of the others.
The IC approves but the AIFM risk function objects.
Under AIFMD the AIFM has the final say on risk; the deal may not proceed.

d: Limited Partner Advisory Committee: a small group of LPs, usually the larger ones, who approve conflicts of interest, review valuation questions and consent to certain waivers. It does not make investment decisions or owe duties to other LPs in most LPAs.
x: Approving a deal between Fund II and a Fund I portfolio company.
Consenting to a one-year term extension.
s: The GP wants to buy an asset from its own previous fund.
The LPAC reviews price, process and fairness opinion before consenting.
An LPAC member is also bidding for the same asset.
That member should declare the conflict and step out of the vote.

d: Individuals named in the LPA whose involvement is a condition of the fund. They must give a stated share of their working time to it. If they leave or fall short, a key person event is triggered.
x: Two founding partners required to spend substantially all business time on the fund.
Three of four named partners must remain for the investment period to continue.
s: One of two key persons leaves in year 2.
The investment period suspends automatically until LPs approve a replacement or vote to continue.
A key person joins a board unrelated to the fund.
Allowed if the time commitment is still met; LPAs often permit limited outside activities.

d: An independent institution that holds assets in custody or verifies ownership, monitors cash flows and checks that the AIFM follows the fund rules. Required for EU AIFs managed by an authorised AIFM.
x: A Luxembourg bank acting as depositary for a RAIF.
A depositary-lite service for a non-EU fund marketed in some EU states.
s: A capital call is paid into an account not monitored by the depositary.
The depositary flags the cash-flow breach; the AIFM must remedy it.
Assets are unlisted shares that cannot be held in custody.
The depositary verifies ownership from share registers and keeps a record.

d: A financial institution that holds securities and cash safely for the fund. Required for certain AIF categories in India and for listed holdings generally.
x: A bank custodian holding a Cat III AIF's listed shares.
A custodian holding shares distributed in kind after an IPO.
s: A Cat III AIF opens a trading account.
SEBI requires a custodian to hold its securities.
A VC fund receives listed shares on IPO.
A custodian account is opened before shares are transferred.

d: Keeps the fund's books, calculates capital accounts and NAV, prepares capital calls and distributions, runs the waterfall and often handles investor KYC and reporting.
x: A Luxembourg administrator producing ILPA quarterly reports.
An Indian fund accountant preparing SEBI quarterly reports.
s: The GP's waterfall model and the administrator's differ.
The two reconcile before any carry is paid; auditors test the result.
An LP asks for its capital account history.
The administrator provides it from the investor ledger.

d: Audits the fund's annual financial statements, including the valuation of unlisted investments, and issues an opinion. Audited accounts are required by LPAs and by many regulations.
x: A Big Four firm auditing a Luxembourg RAIF.
A statutory auditor for a French FPCI.
s: The auditor disagrees with a valuation.
The manager must support its mark with evidence or adjust it before sign-off.
The audit is late.
LPA delivery deadlines (often 120 days) are breached; LPs are notified.

d: A third party that values the fund's investments. Required in some regimes (SEBI AIFs) and used under AIFMD where the AIFM does not run a functionally independent valuation team.
x: A valuation firm preparing semi-annual valuations for an Indian AIF.
An external valuer appointed by an AIFM for a real estate fund.
s: The manager's internal mark is 30% above the valuer's.
The valuation policy sets which figure prevails; large gaps go to the valuation committee.
LPs question a continuation vehicle price.
An independent valuation or fairness opinion supports the price.

d: The person responsible for the manager's compliance programme: policies, monitoring, regulatory filings and training. SEBI requires compliance officers of AIF managers to hold NISM certification.
x: A chief compliance officer at a US registered adviser.
A NISM-certified compliance officer at an Indian AIF manager.
s: A partner wants to trade a listed stock held by the fund.
Personal dealing rules require pre-clearance; the compliance officer blocks or approves.
SEBI asks for evidence of compliance monitoring.
The compliance officer produces the monitoring log and reports.

d: The person responsible for anti-money-laundering controls and reporting suspicions to the financial intelligence unit. Luxembourg calls the role RC (responsable du contrôle).
x: An MLRO reviewing an LP with a complex trust structure.
A Luxembourg RC filing a suspicious transaction report.
s: An LP's source of funds cannot be verified.
The MLRO halts admission until documents are provided or rejects the subscription.
A sanctions list update names an LP's beneficial owner.
The MLRO freezes the account and reports as required.

d: An intermediary paid to introduce LPs to the fund. Its fee is usually borne by the manager or offset against the management fee. Placement agents must be licensed where they operate.
x: Fee of 1.5–2% of capital raised through the agent.
A Monaco CCAF-licensed firm distributing a Luxembourg fund to local clients.
s: The fund pays the agent's fee.
Most LPAs require a 100% offset against the management fee so LPs do not bear it.
An unlicensed introducer contacts a Monaco resident.
This can breach Monaco's canvassing rules.

d: A large early LP whose commitment lets the fund reach first close. Anchors often negotiate fee discounts, co-investment rights or a share of GP economics.
x: A family office committing 25% of target before first close.
A development finance institution anchoring an emerging market fund.
s: An anchor asks for 10% of the carry.
The team weighs dilution against the certainty of reaching first close.
Other LPs ask for the anchor's terms under MFN.
Side letters usually exclude economics tied to commitment size or timing.

d: An experienced operator who works with portfolio companies on strategy, hiring, pricing or operations. Whether their costs are borne by the manager or charged to the fund or companies is a frequent LP question.
x: A former CFO helping portfolio companies with financing.
A pricing specialist working across a buyout portfolio.
s: Operating partner fees are charged to portfolio companies.
LPs ask whether those fees offset the management fee; ILPA templates require disclosure.
A company needs a new CEO.
The operating partner runs the search and may sit on the board.

d: A part-time partner who sources or supports deals, usually without being a key person, paid through deal-level carry or a small retainer.
x: A founder-turned-investor bringing healthtech deals.
A venture partner sitting on two boards.
s: The venture partner sources a deal.
They may receive a share of carry on that deal as agreed.
LPs ask about the venture partner's time.
Not a key person, so no time commitment in the LPA.

d: The function managing communication with LPs: fundraising, reporting, annual meetings and queries. Good IR shortens future fundraises.
x: An IR head handling 80 LPs and the annual meeting.
IR producing the data room and DDQ responses.
s: An LP asks for ad hoc data on portfolio emissions.
IR coordinates with the deal team and answers consistently.
A bad quarter hits.
IR explains marks proactively rather than waiting for questions.

d: The law firm that structures the fund and drafts the LPA, PPM, subscription documents and side letters, and negotiates with LP counsel.
x: A Luxembourg firm drafting an SCSp LPA.
An Indian firm drafting the trust deed and PPM.
s: LP counsel sends 40 pages of comments.
Fund counsel negotiates and tracks agreed points across LPs.
Side letters conflict with each other.
Counsel maintains a register and MFN compendium.

d: The contract that governs the fund: term, investment restrictions, fees, expenses, carry and waterfall, LP rights, key person and removal provisions. Where the PPM and LPA differ, the LPA wins.
x: An 80–150 page LPA for an institutional fund.
An SCSp LPA following the ILPA Model LPA structure.
s: The GP wants to invest in a sector the LPA excludes.
It needs LP consent (often majority by commitment) to amend the restriction.
The PPM says 8% hurdle but the LPA says 7%.
The LPA governs; the PPM error may raise disclosure liability.

d: Template limited partnership agreements published by ILPA, in whole-of-fund and deal-by-deal versions, setting out LP-friendly market terms. Used as a starting point or benchmark in negotiations.
x: An LP sending the ILPA Model LPA as its comment baseline.
A first-time manager drafting from the model to speed LP review.
s: GP and LP disagree on clawback terms.
Both point to the model LPA's clawback provisions as a neutral reference.
A GP departs from the model on removal.
LPs ask why and may request a side letter.

d: The offering document: strategy, team, track record, pipeline, risks and a summary of key terms. It is disclosure and marketing; the LPA is the binding contract. In India it is filed with SEBI through a merchant banker.
x: A 60-page PPM for a European growth fund.
A SEBI-format PPM with mandatory disclosure sections.
s: A risk factor is omitted.
Investors may claim misrepresentation; counsel reviews risk disclosures carefully.
Track record figures differ from the DDQ.
LPs lose trust; all documents should draw on one reconciled data set.

d: A short document listing the fund's main terms (size, fees, carry, hurdle, term, key person, removal) used early in fundraising before the full LPA is shared.
x: A four-page summary sent to anchor prospects.
A summary of terms attached to the PPM.
s: An anchor negotiates off the summary.
Agreed changes flow into the LPA draft.
An LP signs off the summary but objects to the LPA.
The summary is not binding; negotiation continues on the LPA.

d: The document by which an LP commits capital. It holds the commitment amount, investor representations (eligibility, tax status, sanctions), tax forms and KYC information.
x: A subscription booklet with FATCA/CRS forms.
A contribution agreement for an Indian AIF.
s: An LP misstates its accredited status.
It breaches its representations; the GP may compulsorily transfer its interest.
An LP's tax form is missing.
Distributions may be subject to withholding until provided.

d: The Indian AIF equivalent of a subscription agreement and LPA rolled together for each investor, signed with the trustee and manager. It sets commitment, drawdown, fees and investor rights.
x: A contribution agreement for a Cat II AIF with ₹2 crore commitment.
A side letter attached to a contribution agreement.
s: An investor defaults on a drawdown.
The contribution agreement sets the penalty and forfeiture terms.
Terms differ between investors.
SEBI rules and the PPM limit differential rights; they must be disclosed.

d: The document creating an Indian AIF trust: settlor, trustee, beneficiaries, purpose and trustee powers. Registered under the Indian Registration Act.
x: A trust deed settling an AIF with ₹1 lakh initial corpus.
An amendment to the trust deed adding a new scheme.
s: The trustee wants to change the manager.
The trust deed sets the procedure and investor consents.
SEBI asks for the registered deed.
It forms part of the registration application.

d: A separate agreement between the fund and one LP that adds to or varies the LPA for that LP: fee discounts, extra reporting, excuse rights, regulatory protections.
x: A side letter giving a public pension fund transparency on placement agent fees.
A side letter excusing a faith-based LP from alcohol investments.
s: Thirty LPs each have side letters.
Counsel compiles them and runs the MFN process after final close.
A side letter conflicts with the LPA.
Side letters typically override the LPA for that LP only.

d: Most-favoured-nation right in a side letter. The LP may elect terms given to other LPs in their side letters, usually only those of LPs with equal or smaller commitments, and excluding terms tied to an LP's regulatory status.
x: A €20m LP electing a reporting term granted to a €15m LP.
An MFN compendium sent to all LPs after final close.
s: An LP with €5m tries to elect a fee discount given to a €50m LP.
Size-based MFN tiers usually block this.
A term is granted for regulatory reasons.
Most MFNs exclude regulatory-driven terms.

d: Agreement under which the fund, GP or trustee appoints the manager, delegates investment authority and sets the management fee and termination rights.
x: An IMA between a RAIF's AIFM and an investment adviser.
An IMA between an Indian AIF trustee and the manager.
s: The fund wants to terminate the manager.
The IMA sets notice and cause requirements.
Fee calculation disputes arise.
The IMA and LPA definitions control.

d: The standard questionnaire LPs send to a GP during fundraising, covering firm, team, strategy, operations, compliance and ESG. ILPA publishes a widely used template.
x: An ILPA DDQ completed for a Fund II raise.
An ODD questionnaire focused on cybersecurity.
s: Fifteen LPs send their own DDQs.
The GP answers the ILPA DDQ once and maps answers to each LP's format.
An answer changes mid-raise.
The GP updates all LPs to keep disclosures consistent.

d: A secure online repository of fund documents for prospective LPs: PPM, LPA, track record, policies, references and DDQ. Access logs show who read what.
x: A virtual data room with 200 documents for Fund III.
A deal data room for a portfolio company sale.
s: An LP downloads only the track record.
IR follows up on that interest.
A document is updated.
Version control prevents LPs relying on outdated drafts.

d: A three-page EU disclosure document required when packaged products are offered to retail investors, covering risk, costs and performance scenarios. Needed for ELTIFs and other funds sold to EU retail.
x: A KID for an ELTIF sold through private banks.
A KID for an FPCI marketed to €30,000 investors.
s: A fund adds retail investors.
A KID must be produced before retail distribution.
Performance scenarios look misleading.
Methodology follows PRIIPs rules; managers add narrative where allowed.

d: Notice to LPs to pay a stated part of their commitment by a deadline, usually about ten business days, with the purpose of the call and the LP's share.
x: A notice calling 8% of commitments for a new investment and fees.
An ILPA-format capital call notice.
s: An LP pays late.
Default interest and remedies under the LPA apply.
A call purpose changes after issue.
The GP explains to LPs; cash may be held or returned.

d: Notice to LPs of a distribution: amount, source (exit, income), waterfall tier, any withholding and whether it is recallable.
x: A notice distributing €12m from a trade sale.
A notice of in-kind distribution of listed shares.
s: Part of a distribution is recallable.
The notice says so, so LPs know it adds back to unfunded commitments.
Tax is withheld for one LP.
The notice shows gross, withholding and net amounts.

d: Periodic statement of one LP's contributions, distributions, fees, allocated gains and losses, and ending balance.
x: A quarterly ILPA-format capital account statement.
An annual audited capital account.
s: An LP's statement shows unrealised gains.
These are paper gains until exits occur.
Two LPs have different fees.
Each capital account reflects its own fee terms.

d: Guidance from the Institutional Limited Partners Association on fund terms, governance and transparency (ILPA Principles 3.0), plus standard templates. The Reporting Template was updated in January 2025 for use from Q1 2026; a new Performance Template applies to funds starting from 2026.
x: A GP reporting fees, expenses and carry using the 2025 ILPA Reporting Template.
An LP benchmarking an LPA against ILPA Principles 3.0.
s: A fund launched in 2026 asks which template to use.
ILPA recommends the updated Reporting Template and the Performance Template for funds starting operations from 1 January 2026.
A GP's fund left its investment period in 2024.
It may continue with the 2016 template or adopt the new one.

d: The rules the manager follows to value unlisted investments each quarter: methods, sources, frequency, governance and who signs off.
x: A policy adopting IPEV methods with a valuation committee.
A SEBI-compliant policy with independent valuer reviews.
s: A portfolio company raises a round at a higher price.
The policy says how much weight the new price gets in fair value.
Markets fall but no transactions occur.
The policy requires adjusting comparables rather than holding cost.

d: The document showing how each investment's fair value was reached: method, inputs, comparables and judgment. Auditors and LPs review it.
x: A quarterly report valuing 20 companies on multiples.
An independent valuer's report for a continuation vehicle.
s: An LP asks why a mark rose 40%.
The report shows the new round price and the adjustments made.
The auditor challenges a discount rate.
The report must justify inputs with evidence.

d: The manager's written approach to identifying, recording and managing conflicts, including allocation between funds, related-party deals, fees from portfolio companies and personal interests.
x: A policy requiring LPAC consent for cross-fund investments.
An allocation policy annex for funds with overlapping strategies.
s: Two funds want the same deal.
The policy's allocation rules decide the split.
A partner's relative owns a target company.
The partner declares and recuses; the conflict is logged.

d: The manager's procedures for verifying investors and beneficial owners, screening sanctions, monitoring transactions and reporting suspicions, scaled to risk.
x: A risk-based KYC policy with enhanced checks for politically exposed persons.
An AML policy aligned with FATF Recommendations.
s: An LP is a trust with layered companies.
Enhanced due diligence traces ultimate beneficial owners.
A regulator inspects AML files.
The policy and evidence must match.

d: International Private Equity and Venture Capital Valuation Guidelines: the common fair value framework, using methods such as recent transaction price, multiples and discounted cash flow, consistent with IFRS 13 and ASC 820.
x: A VC fund calibrating marks to the last round under IPEV.
A buyout fund using EV/EBITDA multiples.
s: A round was 18 months ago.
IPEV says the price must be recalibrated for changes since, not held.
A company misses plan badly.
Fair value falls even without a new round.
